newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Gore meets S.Korean president over peace drive.
newsitem.headline: Gore meets S.Korean president over peace drive.

text.p: U.S. Vice-President Al Gore held private talks on Saturday with South Korean President Kim Young-sam to discuss ways to convince North Korea to join four-nation peace talks.
"These discussions take place at a very important time," Gore told Kim at the start of the talks at the presidential Blue House.

International aid agencies say North Korea is weeks away from starvation, and in what South Korea regards as evidence of its desperation has offered to join peace talks if Seoul and Washington first agree to supply substantial food aid.
The United States and South Korea reject any preconditions for talks but are dropping hints they could do more to relieve the North's suffering once it sits at the peace table.

"I hope that the proposed four-party talks will be realised soon so that the grave difficulties North Korea is facing will be alleviated," Kim told Gore, according to a text of his comments released in Seoul.
Kim made no direct reference to aid. The United States and South Korea have agreed to chip in $10 million and $6 million respectively to the latest U.N. food appeal for North Korea.
Kim said Seoul and Washington "are cooperating even more closely with each other than ever before to establish durable peace on the Korean peninsula".

The United States has been trying to convince North Korea to accept a proposal for talks between North and South Korea, the United States and China put forward by U.S. President Bill Clinton and Kim last April.

The talks would be aimed initially at securing a lasting peace to replace the armistice that ended the 1950-1953 Korean War, which the United States believes would serve as a springboard for ending tensions on the peninsula.
After his talks on Saturday with Kim, Gore was to visit the Demilitarized Zone separating the North and South and meet some of the 37,000 U.S. troops stationed in South Korea.
Gore, who spent five days in China before arriving in Korea on Friday, discussed the talks during his meetings with Chinese President Jiang Zemin, U.S. officials said.
North Korea has been devastated by two consecutive years of floods, and there are reports its citizens have been reduced to foraging for tree bark and edible grass to survive.

South Korea harbours intense mistrust towards North Korea and takes a hard line on aid and economic contacts. The United States is more actively seeking engagement to try to engineer a "soft landing" for the impoverished nation.
According to a senior U.S. official involved in Gore's talks with Kim, "the United States and South Korea are not willing to have a precondition for entry into four-party talks".
But he said North Korea had been told if it participated in the talks "there will be a great deal of goodwill ... good things will happen."
The official, noting that the United States had supplied humanitarian aid to the North, said additional supplies could be sent once talks began.
While Gore was in South Korea, a five-member delegation of U.S. senators, led by Ted Stevens, the chairman of the Senate Approprations Committee, was in Pyongyang for talks.

The delegation met Kim before departing on their mission. Accompanying Stevens were Republicans Pete Domenici of New Mexico, Thad Cochran of Mississippi, Pat Roberts of Kansas and Democrat Daniel Inouye of Hawaii.
